name: Mercedes-Benz 190E EVO II V8
description:
When Mercedes-Benz introduced the compact W201 190 series in 1982, few could have predicted it would evolve into one of the most legendary homologation specials in motorsport history. Affectionately nicknamed the 'Baby-Benz,' the 190 would prove that compact didn't mean compromised, especially when racing ambitions dictated its development path.

The 190 E 2.5-16 Evolution II made its dramatic debut at the 1990 Geneva Motor Show, representing the ultimate expression of Mercedes' DTM (Deutsche Tourenwagen Masters) racing program. To meet homologation requirements, Mercedes produced exactly 502 road-going examples—each one a rolling testament to motorsport engineering. The EVO II was instantly recognizable: a massive adjustable rear wing that could generate significant downforce, aggressively flared wheel arches accommodating wider tracks, and a front splitter that announced serious aerodynamic intent. This wasn't subtle—it was a race car for the street.

While the original EVO II came with a highly-tuned 2.5-liter inline-four producing 235 horsepower, this V8-swapped variant takes the concept to an entirely different level. The original four-cylinder has been replaced with a naturally aspirated 4.0-liter V8 producing a staggering 502 horsepower at 8,500 rpm and 452 Nm of torque at 5,800 rpm. This screaming 32-valve V8 maintains the naturally aspirated purity of the original concept while multiplying the performance exponentially. Power flows through a close-ratio 6-speed manual transmission to the rear wheels—a setup that demands skill and rewards precision.

The transformation is remarkable. What was already a homologation special capable of embarrassing supercars has become a compact demon that combines DTM-inspired aerodynamics with modern supercar power. At just 1,410 kg, the power-to-weight ratio of 2.81 kg/hp enables acceleration under 4.5 seconds to 100 km/h and a top speed exceeding 320 km/h. The chassis retains the EVO II's competition-oriented suspension geometry, with wider tracks, stiffer spring rates, and upgraded brakes to handle the additional performance.

This V8 EVO II represents the ultimate 'what if'—what if Mercedes had decided to truly unleash the Baby-Benz without constraint? The result is a car that honors the original EVO II's racing heritage while delivering performance that would have dominated not just DTM but the entire supercar landscape of the early 1990s. It's a perfect marriage of homologation special pedigree and modern performance engineering.
